clinicalPearls: WHO operationally defines osteoporosis as a bone density T-score of -2.5 or below (>=2.5 SD below the young-adult mean for same sex/race), measured at lumbar spine, total hip, or femoral neck; osteopenia (low bone density) is a T-score of -1.0 to -2.5 and is a risk factor for developing osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291).

A fragility fracture (hip or vertebral) by definition establishes osteoporosis and warrants treatment, regardless of the T-score; patients presenting with hip or spine fractures by definition have osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298).
Osteoporosis is most common among postmenopausal women, but ~30% of fragility fractures occur in men; secondary osteoporosis arises from other underlying diseases (Harrison 22e p.3291).

>50% of fractures, including hip fractures, among postmenopausal women occur in individuals with osteopenia rather than densitometric osteoporosis, because that population is much larger - hence the shift toward absolute fracture-risk assessment (Harrison 22e p.3291).

FRAX and the Garvan Fracture Risk Calculator estimate 10-year probability of hip or major osteoporotic fracture by combining age, sex, and clinical risk factors with or without BMD, and inform country-specific intervention thresholds distinct from diagnostic thresholds (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298).
Glucocorticoids are the most common cause of medication-induced osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3296).
Any fracture (excluding fingers, toes, face, skull) in a woman aged >50 or a man aged >60 should trigger investigation for osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3293).
harrison.pathophysiology: Osteoporosis is reduced bone strength leading to skeletal fragility and fractures; BMD alone underestimates fragility because microarchitectural deterioration and component misalignment also contribute. A low peak bone mass (genetic, hormonal, nutritional) may underlie disease, with superimposed age-related and extrinsic changes in bone remodeling. In adults remodeling (not modeling) predominates and serves to repair microdamage and supply calcium. Estrogen deficiency drives bone loss by (1) activating new remodeling sites and (2) creating an imbalance favoring resorption over formation: loss of estrogen increases RANKL and reduces osteoprotegerin, increasing osteoclast formation/recruitment, while shortening osteoblast life span and prolonging osteoclast longevity/activity. Trabecular bone (80% of surface area) is preferentially affected, so vertebral fractures are the earliest skeletal consequence. Estrogen also regulates remodeling in men. Heritability of BMD is ~50-80%; LRP5 activating mutations cause high bone mass and inactivating mutations cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3293-3295).

Significant height loss (>4 cm) suggesting occult vertebral fracture
Hip fracture - high mortality (20-25% die within the year) and major loss of independence
More chronic severe pain after vertebral fracture should raise suspicion of multiple myeloma or other underlying bone condition
harrison.prognosis: Lifetime osteoporotic fracture risk for a 50-year-old Caucasian woman is ~50% and ~25% for a man; lifetime hip fracture probability ~14% (women) and ~5% (men), roughly half for African Americans. Hip fractures carry high morbidity and mortality with 20-25% of patients dying within the year (higher among men and African Americans), and ~30% of survivors requiring long-term care, many never regaining prior independence. A first fracture exponentially increases risk of further fracture, especially in the first year; almost 20% of women sustain a second fracture within 2 years (Harrison 22e p.3291-3293).
pitfalls: Failing to exclude secondary causes of osteoporosis (e.g. myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, Cushing's, malabsorption/celiac, hypogonadism, mastocytosis) before attributing low bone mass to primary disease, particularly in patients with fractures or unexpectedly low Z-scores.

Excluding a patient from osteoporosis evaluation simply because a fracture was traumatic - patients with osteoporosis are also more likely to sustain traumatic fractures, and any fracture warrants skeletal assessment.

Relying solely on BMD, which can underestimate fragility (microarchitectural deterioration not captured) and is falsely elevated in the spine by osteoarthritic bone spurs/spondylosis; small slim people show falsely low DXA values.
Fewer than 20% of fracture patients are investigated or treated for osteoporosis within 6 months; postfracture care remains fragmented.
Drug holidays are appropriate to consider for oral/IV bisphosphonates but should be avoided for denosumab and anabolic agents because of more rapid offset.
harrison.severityClassification: WHO densitometric categories: normal (T-score >= -1.0), osteopenia/low bone density (T-score -1.0 to -2.5), osteoporosis (T-score <= -2.5 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip). Presence of a fragility fracture (notably hip or vertebral) defines established/clinical osteoporosis regardless of T-score. Absolute fracture risk (FRAX/Garvan 10-year hip and major osteoporotic fracture probability) is increasingly used alongside or instead of T-score for treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3297-3298).
management: First-line antiresorptive therapy with bisphosphonates, or denosumab where bisphosphonates are unsuitable, to reduce fracture risk
Anabolic agents such as teriparatide or romosozumab for very high fracture risk, followed by an antiresorptive to consolidate the gains
Ensure calcium and vitamin D repletion, weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise, smoking cessation and moderation of alcohol
Fall-prevention measures with correction of visual and gait hazards to avert fragility fractures
Identify and treat secondary causes, minimise glucocorticoid exposure, and consider oestrogen or a selective oestrogen-receptor modulator in appropriate postmenopausal women
Base treatment decisions on absolute fracture-risk assessment such as FRAX and monitor response with serial DXA
Consider a drug holiday after prolonged bisphosphonate therapy, and avoid abrupt denosumab discontinuation without a follow-on antiresorptive to prevent rebound vertebral fractures
